primary.title: Four generations of Decap organ builders in Herentals

intro.text: Aloïs Decap started renting out organs around Antwerp in 1895. His son Frans founded Decap Herentals in 1933. Today Tony Decap, the fourth generation, builds dance organs, orchestrions, self-playing instruments and the technology that drives them in the same town.

primary.title: One family, one trade, since 1895

body.text: Decap Herentals is known for real dance organs: organs built for people to dance to. We have built street organs and barrel organs too, but dance organs are what we normally make. The workshop is on the Langepad in Herentals, Belgium.

The trade has passed from father to son four times. Each generation kept what worked and changed what no longer did: Frans gave the business its own workshop, François took the dance organ digital, and Tony brought MIDI and then smARTvalve.

primary.title: We learned woodworking to build organs

body.text: At heart we are musicians, not carpenters. We learned to work wood so we could build organs, but the music comes first. That set Decap apart then, and it still does.

Between 1960 and 1980, the golden age of the dance organ, there were some 120 dance cafés and dance halls across Belgium where people went to dance every day, each with its own dance organ. Since Decap Herentals began, we have chased one thing: an organ that plays better. More feeling, more control over volume and intensity, more dynamics, more musicality.

items.title: The first to bring MIDI to the organ

body.text: Tony Decap brings MIDI to the organ. A whole music library fits on one digital card and replaces racks of cardboard music books. In the years that follow Decap builds more than dance organs: orchestrions, separate pipe chest units, automatic drums and other self-playing instruments.

intro.text: The milestones below come from family records and from the history of the Decap family published by Mostmans in Carousel Organ no. 4 (2000).

primary.title: Two Decap workshops, one founder

body.text: Two organ businesses carry the Decap name today, and both descend from Aloïs Decap.
Gebroeders Decap Antwerpen (Decap Brothers, Antwerp) continues from the partnership Aloïs's sons formed in Antwerp after the First World War.
Decap Herentals goes back to 1933, when Frans Decap set up his own workshop in Herentals. This is the Decap you are reading about.

The two companies are independent of each other and on friendly terms. If you have a Decap organ and are not sure which workshop built it, send us a photo of the façade and any nameplate. We will tell you what we can.

primary.title: Frank Decap and his Atelier

body.text: Frank Decap is Tony's brother. He runs his own business, Atelier Frank Decap, as a master craftsman dedicated to organ restoration, working the way earlier generations of the family did.
Frank also installs our MIDI conversion units, so a restored book organ can play from books and from MIDI. Restoration enquiries go straight to him through his page on this site.

primary.title: From the CNC to the player, made in Herentals

body.text: Almost everything that goes into a Decap organ is made under our own roof. All our software is our own: the CNC programs that mill the pipes, the software that drives the instruments and the player that plays them.
